distinctions.note: His later, fuller study following the order of the Divine Liturgy.
As an ordinary phrase it echoes John 6:51; as a capitalized title it names the book.

collocations: Schmemann's For the Life of the World
read For the Life of the World
in For the Life of the World
the argument of For the Life of the World

examples.everyday: If you're curious about Orthodoxy, start with For the Life of the World; it's short and beautiful.
examples.professional: For next week, read the first two chapters of For the Life of the World and come ready to discuss Schmemann's idea of secularism.
examples.analytical: In For the Life of the World, the Eucharist is not one religious act among others but the key to what the whole world is for.

nuance.etymology: From John 6:51, where Jesus says the bread he will give for the life of the world is his flesh.
common_mistakes: Italicizing or capitalizing it when using the biblical phrase in ordinary prose.
Calling it Schmemann's dissertation; it is a popular book.
nuance.biblical_note: The title quotes John 6:51, in the Bread of Life discourse, where Jesus says that the bread he will give for the life of the world is his flesh. Schmemann reads the verse as the meaning of the Eucharist: Christ's self-offering is for the whole world, not for a religious section of it.

senses: The last Sunday before Orthodox Great Lent, ending with a service where everyone asks and gives forgiveness to one another.

etymology: English “forgiveness” + “Sunday,” from the rite of mutual forgiveness held that evening.

core.definition: The last Sunday before Orthodox Great Lent, ending with a service where everyone asks and gives forgiveness to one another.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GIV in forgiveness and SUN in Sunday; the first syllable “for” is weak, almost “fer.”

nuance.usage_note: Also called Cheesefare Sunday, the last day dairy is eaten before Lent; the day also remembers Adam's expulsion from Paradise, and the Gospel is Matthew 6:14-21. At the evening Forgiveness Vespers, Lenten tones and colors begin; afterward each person bows to every other person saying “Forgive me,” with the reply “God forgives” (or “I forgive; forgive me”). The next day is Clean Monday.

distinctions.note: Cheesefare Sunday is the same day named for its fasting rule.
Ash Wednesday is the Western beginning of Lent, with ashes; Orthodox Lent begins on Clean Monday, after Forgiveness Sunday.
Meatfare Sunday, a week earlier, is the last day for meat and is devoted to the Last Judgment.

examples.everyday: Don't skip Vespers on Forgiveness Sunday; bowing to everyone and saying “forgive me” is the real start of Lent.
examples.professional: In my Forgiveness Sunday homily I'll connect Adam's exile from Paradise with our need to be reconciled before the fast.
examples.analytical: Forgiveness Sunday places reconciliation before fasting, showing that ascetic effort without love is spiritually empty.

nuance.analogy: Clearing the road of fallen trees before a long journey.
nuance.etymology: English “forgiveness” + “Sunday,” from the rite of mutual forgiveness held that evening.
common_mistakes: Answering “Forgive me” with “It's okay”; the traditional reply is “God forgives” or “I forgive; forgive me.”
Thinking Lent starts on Ash Wednesday in the Orthodox Church.
nuance.biblical_note: The Gospel for the day, Matthew 6:14-21, joins Jesus' words that the Father forgives those who forgive others with his teaching on fasting in secret and laying up treasure in heaven.

senses: The solemn Orthodox rite of blessing water on Theophany and its eve, celebrating Christ's baptism and the sanctifying of creation.

etymology: English rendering of Greek Megas Hagiasmos, “Great Sanctification.”

core.definition: The solemn Orthodox rite of blessing water on Theophany and its eve, celebrating Christ's baptism and the sanctifying of creation.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GREAT, BLESS and WA-; the t in “waters” is a flap, so it sounds like “WAW-derz.”

nuance.usage_note: Served after the Liturgy on the eve of Theophany (January 5) and on the feast itself (January 6), with Old Testament and New Testament readings and the great prayer “Great art Thou, O Lord,” traditionally attributed to Saint Sophronius of Jerusalem. The priest immerses the cross three times while the troparion of Theophany is sung. Many American parishes also bless a river, lake or the ocean, and in Greek communities young people dive for the cross. The faithful take the water home to drink, and priests use it to bless homes.

distinctions.note: The Lesser Blessing of Waters is a shorter rite that may be served at any time, for example at the start of the month or on August 1.
Baptism is the sacrament of a person; the Great Blessing sanctifies water and, through it, creation.
Holy water is the result; the Great Blessing is the rite that makes Theophany water.

collocations: the Great Blessing of Waters at Theophany
serve the Great Blessing of Waters
the prayer of the Great Blessing of Waters

examples.everyday: Bring an empty bottle on Sunday; after the Great Blessing of Waters you can take some home.
examples.professional: This year our parish will serve the Great Blessing of Waters at the lake, followed by house blessings throughout January.
examples.analytical: The Great Blessing of Waters proclaims that in Christ's baptism the material world itself is restored as a means of communion with God.

nuance.etymology: English rendering of Greek Megas Hagiasmos, “Great Sanctification.”
common_mistakes: Calling it a baptism; nobody is baptized in this rite.
Thinking it happens only once on the eve; it is usually served on both the eve and the feast.
nuance.biblical_note: The rite celebrates Christ's baptism in the Jordan in Matthew 3:13-17, Mark 1:9-11 and Luke 3:21-22, where the Spirit descends like a dove and the Father's voice is heard. Its readings include Isaiah 12:3, about drawing water with joy from the wells of salvation.

senses: The long, penitential form of the Byzantine bedtime service, served on weekday evenings of Great Lent and on the eves of Nativity and Theophany.

etymology: English “compline” from Old French complie, from Latin completa (hora), “the completed hour”; Greek apodeipnon, “after supper.”

core.definition: The long, penitential form of the Byzantine bedtime service, served on weekday evenings of Great Lent and on the eves of Nativity and Theophany.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the first syllable of Compline, KAHM; Americans say it to rhyme with “COM-plin,” not “com-PLINE.”

nuance.connotation: positive; quiet, penitential and beloved by many Orthodox Christians.
nuance.usage_note: Great Compline (Greek Mega Apodeipnon) is served Monday through Thursday in Great Lent and on a few feast eves. In the first week of Lent it includes the Great Canon of Saint Andrew of Crete, read in four parts. Its hallmarks are the hymn “God is with us” from Isaiah, the prayer of Saint Ephrem with prostrations and, in Lent, the hymn “O Lord of hosts, be with us.”

distinctions.note: Small Compline is the short form used on most evenings of the year.
Vespers opens the liturgical day at sunset; Compline is said after supper before sleep.
The Great Canon is a long hymn read within Great Compline in the first week of Lent, not a separate service.

collocations: Great Compline with the Great Canon
Great Compline in the first week of Lent

examples.everyday: Great Compline is on Monday at six thirty; it's long, but the candlelit church is beautiful.
examples.professional: Choir directors should remind singers that “God is with us” at Great Compline alternates with verses from Isaiah.
examples.analytical: Great Compline frames the night as a time of spiritual struggle, asking God's protection before sleep, an image of death.

nuance.etymology: English “compline” from Old French complie, from Latin completa (hora), “the completed hour”; Greek apodeipnon, “after supper.”
common_mistakes: Saying “com-PLINE”; the stress is on the first syllable.
Assuming Great Compline is served every day of the year.
nuance.biblical_note: The service's opening hymn, “God is with us,” is built from Isaiah 8:9-18 and 9:2, 6-7, ending with the prophecy of the child born to us whose name is Wonderful Counselor, Mighty God.

senses: The hymn beginning “Glory to God in the highest,” sung near the end of Sunday and festal Matins in the Byzantine rite.

etymology: Greek doxologia, from doxa “glory” + logos “word”; “great” distinguishes it from the short doxology.

core.definition: The hymn beginning “Glory to God in the highest,” sung near the end of Sunday and festal Matins in the Byzantine rite.

pronunciation.tip: Stress the second syllable of Doxology, SAHL; the x sounds like “ks.”

nuance.usage_note: In Byzantine Matins the Great Doxology follows the Praises; on Sundays and feasts it is sung, opening with “Glory to Thee who hast shown us the light,” and is followed by the Trisagion and the troparion of the day. On ordinary weekdays a slightly different form is read, often called the “read” or “small” doxology. In the West the same hymn is the Gloria in excelsis of the Mass. For many Americans, “the Doxology” means the Protestant hymn “Praise God from whom all blessings flow,” which is different.

distinctions.note: The Gloria is the Western liturgical name for essentially the same hymn, sung at Mass.
The small or lesser doxology is “Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit.”
In many American Protestant churches “the Doxology” means Thomas Ken's hymn “Praise God from whom all blessings flow.”

collocations: the Great Doxology and the Trisagion
a setting of the Great Doxology

examples.everyday: When the choir starts the Great Doxology, I know Matins is almost over and the Liturgy will begin soon.
examples.professional: The Great Doxology greets the dawn, so in monasteries it is timed to coincide with sunrise.
examples.analytical: The Great Doxology joins the angels' song at Bethlehem to the Church's morning praise, making each Sunday dawn a celebration of the light of Christ.

nuance.etymology: Greek doxologia, from doxa “glory” + logos “word”; “great” distinguishes it from the short doxology.
common_mistakes: Confusing it with “the Doxology” sung in Protestant churches.
Stressing Doxology on the first syllable.
nuance.biblical_note: The hymn opens with the angels' praise in Luke 2:14 and goes on to address Christ in words echoing John 1:29 as the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world.

senses: The solemn procession in the Divine Liturgy in which the bread and wine are carried from the table of preparation to the altar.

etymology: Translation of Greek Megalē Eisodos, “great entrance.”

core.definition: The solemn procession in the Divine Liturgy in which the bread and wine are carried from the table of preparation to the altar.

pronunciation.tip: Stress EN in Entrance (the noun); the verb entrance (to delight) is stressed on the second syllable.

nuance.usage_note: During the Cherubic Hymn the deacon and priest take the gifts from the prothesis table, go out through the north door, and return through the Royal Doors, commemorating the Church's hierarchy, civil authorities and the faithful. Then the gifts are placed on the holy table. At the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts the Great Entrance carries the already consecrated gifts, in silence, while the people kneel or prostrate. The Western parallel is the presentation of the gifts at the offertory.

distinctions.note: The Little Entrance carries the Gospel book, earlier in the Liturgy.
In the Roman Mass lay people may bring up the gifts; the Byzantine Great Entrance is a clergy procession.
Procession is any ceremonial movement; the Great Entrance is one specific procession.

collocations: the Great Entrance with the gifts
the commemorations at the Great Entrance
the Cherubic Hymn and the Great Entrance

examples.everyday: When should I stand back at the Great Entrance? Right when the choir pauses in the Cherubic Hymn.
examples.professional: Altar servers carry candles at the Great Entrance and walk ahead of the deacon.
examples.analytical: Byzantine commentators read the Great Entrance as Christ's procession to his Passion and burial, though historically it began as a practical transfer of the gifts.

nuance.etymology: Translation of Greek Megalē Eisodos, “great entrance.”
common_mistakes: Calling it a consecration; the gifts are not yet consecrated at the Great Entrance (except at the Presanctified Liturgy).
Stressing “enTRANCE” as in the verb.

senses: The opening series of deacon's petitions, beginning “In peace let us pray to the Lord,” each answered “Lord, have mercy.”

etymology: Greek litaneia “supplication,” from litē “prayer, entreaty”; “great” translates megalē.

core.definition: The opening series of deacon's petitions, beginning “In peace let us pray to the Lord,” each answered “Lord, have mercy.”

pronunciation.tip: Stress LIT; the t is a flap, so it sounds like “LID-uh-nee.”

nuance.usage_note: Also called the Litany of Peace (Greek Megalē Synaptē). It opens the Divine Liturgy, Vespers, Matins and most sacraments, with petitions for peace, the Church, clergy, the nation, travelers, the sick and more. Note that in the Anglican Book of Common Prayer “the Great Litany” means a different text, Cranmer's 1544 litany in English.

distinctions.note: The Augmented (Fervent) Litany has a triple “Lord, have mercy” and intercessions for specific people.
The Small Litany is a short three-petition litany repeated through services.
The Anglican Great Litany is Cranmer's English litany, unrelated in text.

collocations: the Great Litany at the beginning of the Liturgy
the petitions of the Great Litany

examples.everyday: If you get there late, you'll miss the Great Litany, where the deacon prays for everything from the weather to travelers.
examples.professional: In the Great Litany the deacon leads the people's prayer, while the priest says a separate prayer quietly.
examples.analytical: The Great Litany shows that the Church begins worship by gathering the whole world into its intercession.

nuance.etymology: Greek litaneia “supplication,” from litē “prayer, entreaty”; “great” translates megalē.
common_mistakes: Calling every litany “the Great Litany.”
Assuming the Anglican Great Litany is the same text.

senses: The fuller, festal form of the Byzantine evening service, served on Saturday evenings and on the eves of feasts.

etymology: Latin vesper “evening,” used for the Greek Hesperinos.

core.definition: The fuller, festal form of the Byzantine evening service, served on Saturday evenings and on the eves of feasts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VES; the ending is an American r-colored “perz.”

nuance.usage_note: Great Vespers includes the evening Psalm 103 (LXX numbering), “Lord, I have cried” with festal hymns, an entrance with the censer, “O Gladsome Light,” the prokeimenon and, on feasts, Old Testament readings. When part of an all-night vigil it may add the litiya, with blessing of bread, wheat, wine and oil. Daily Vespers, served on ordinary weekdays, lacks the entrance and readings. In American parishes, Saturday evening Great Vespers is the main weekly service besides the Sunday Liturgy.

distinctions.note: Daily Vespers is the simpler weekday form, without the entrance.
The all-night vigil joins Great Vespers and Matins into one service.
A Vesperal Liturgy is Vespers combined with the Divine Liturgy, as on Holy Thursday.

examples.everyday: Confession is after Great Vespers on Saturday, so come around five.
examples.professional: At Great Vespers the entrance with the censer accompanies “O Gladsome Light.”
examples.analytical: Great Vespers begins the liturgical day at sunset, so Sunday's resurrection praise begins on Saturday evening.

nuance.etymology: Latin vesper “evening,” used for the Greek Hesperinos.
common_mistakes: Calling every Vespers “Great Vespers.”
Thinking the day starts at midnight; liturgically it starts with Vespers.

senses: The altar table in the center of an Orthodox sanctuary, on which the Eucharist is celebrated and the Gospel book rests.

etymology: Translation of Greek hagia trapeza.

core.definition: The altar table in the center of an Orthodox sanctuary, on which the Eucharist is celebrated and the Gospel book rests.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HO and TA; the final syllable of “table” is a soft “bul.”

nuance.usage_note: Greek hagia trapeza; Slavonic prestol (“throne”). It holds the antimension, Gospel book, tabernacle and blessing cross, and is consecrated by a bishop, often with relics. Only the clergy touch it. In Orthodox usage the whole sanctuary is often called the altar, so “holy table” avoids confusion. Anglicans also speak of the “holy table.”

distinctions.note: In Orthodox speech “the altar” usually means the whole sanctuary, while “holy table” is the table itself.
The table of oblation (prothesis) is the side table where the gifts are prepared.
Communion table is the usual Protestant term, stressing a meal rather than a sacrifice.

collocations: the holy table and the antimension

examples.everyday: Altar servers never put anything on the holy table; only the priest and deacon handle it.
examples.professional: During the consecration of a church, the bishop washes and anoints the holy table with chrism.
examples.analytical: The holy table is both tomb and throne: Christ's death and his reign meet there.

nuance.etymology: Translation of Greek hagia trapeza.
common_mistakes: Using “altar” for the table when Orthodox mean the whole sanctuary.
Thinking lay people may touch it.

senses: The priest's exclamation before Communion as he lifts the consecrated Lamb, inviting only the holy, God's people, to the Holy Gifts.

etymology: Translation of Greek Ta hagia tois hagiois.

core.definition: The priest's exclamation before Communion as he lifts the consecrated Lamb, inviting only the holy, God's people, to the Holy Gifts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HO, THINGS and HO; “for the” is quick, “fer thuh.”

nuance.usage_note: Greek Ta hagia tois hagiois, Slavonic Svyataya svyatym. The people respond, “One is holy, one is Lord, Jesus Christ, to the glory of God the Father.” Older English translations read “The holy things unto the holy.” It is often explained in sermons: no one is holy on his own, but those made holy by Christ receive him.

distinctions.note: The Roman Mass's invitation to Communion; its function is similar but its wording differs.
The deacon's call to attention just before this exclamation.
The later invitation, “With fear of God and faith, draw near,” calls the people to come forward.

collocations: the elevation at “Holy things for the holy”
the response to “Holy things for the holy”
“Holy things for the holy” and “One is holy”

examples.everyday: When Father says “Holy things for the holy,” I always feel unworthy, and then we sing “One is holy,” which helps.
examples.professional: In today's homily I'll explain why the Church answers “Holy things for the holy” with “One is holy.”
examples.analytical: “Holy things for the holy” presents holiness as received rather than achieved: the saints are those made holy by the One who is holy.

nuance.etymology: Translation of Greek Ta hagia tois hagiois.
common_mistakes: Thinking it excludes everyone not morally perfect; in context it calls the baptized faithful to Communion.
Responding with the wrong words; the response is “One is holy, one is Lord, Jesus Christ.”
nuance.biblical_note: The people's response echoes Philippians 2:11, where every tongue confesses that Jesus Christ is Lord, to the glory of God the Father.

senses: The Thursday of Holy Week, commemorating the Last Supper, the institution of the Eucharist, the washing of feet and the betrayal.

etymology: English “holy” + Thursday, “Thor's day.”

core.definition: The Thursday of Holy Week, commemorating the Last Supper, the institution of the Eucharist, the washing of feet and the betrayal.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HO and THURS; the th is voiceless, and in fast speech Americans say “THURZ-dee.”

nuance.usage_note: In Byzantine practice Great and Holy Thursday has a Vesperal Liturgy of Saint Basil in the morning, with the hymn “Of thy Mystical Supper.” In cathedrals and monasteries the bishop or abbot may wash feet; reserved Communion for the sick is often prepared for the year; and when needed the Patriarch consecrates holy chrism. The evening Matins of Holy Friday includes the Twelve Passion Gospels. Catholics and many Protestants call it Maundy Thursday, with the Mass of the Lord's Supper and foot washing.

distinctions.note: Maundy Thursday is the usual Western English name, from Latin mandatum (“commandment”), recalling John 13:34.
Ascension Thursday comes forty days after Easter, not in Holy Week.
Good Friday commemorates the crucifixion the next day.

collocations: the Twelve Gospels on Holy Thursday

examples.everyday: Holy Thursday is a long day: Liturgy in the morning, then the Twelve Gospels at night.
examples.professional: On Holy Thursday the troparion contrasts Judas, who loved money, with the disciples enlightened at the supper.
examples.analytical: Holy Thursday holds together the gift of the Eucharist and the betrayal, so communion and treachery stand at the same table.

nuance.etymology: English “holy” + Thursday, “Thor's day.”
common_mistakes: Confusing it with Ascension Thursday.
Saying “Holy Thirsday”; spell Thursday with u.
nuance.biblical_note: The day follows the Last Supper in Matthew 26:17-29, Mark 14:12-25 and Luke 22:7-23, and Paul's account of the institution in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26. John 13:1-15 tells of Jesus washing the disciples' feet, and the arrest is told in John 18:1-12.

senses: The sacrament of anointing the sick with blessed oil and prayer, for healing of body and soul and forgiveness of sins.

etymology: Latin unctio “anointing,” from ungere “to anoint.”

core.definition: The sacrament of anointing the sick with blessed oil and prayer, for healing of body and soul and forgiveness of sins.

pronunciation.tip: Stress HO and UNC; “unction” sounds like “UNGK-shun,” with the n said as “ng.”

nuance.usage_note: The usual English name in Orthodox parishes for the Mystery called euchelaion in Greek and soborovanie in Russian. The priest may serve it at a hospital bedside or at home, and many parishes serve it for all the faithful on Holy Wednesday or during Great Lent. In general American English, “unction” alone can also mean an exaggerated, oily manner of speaking, so use the full phrase.

distinctions.note: Euchelaion is the Greek name for the same sacrament.
Last rites is a Catholic expression for the sacraments given to the dying, including anointing, confession and viaticum.
Chrismation is anointing with chrism after baptism; holy unction is for the sick.

collocations: serve holy unction at the hospital

examples.everyday: Grandma's surgery is on Friday, so Father is coming Thursday to give her holy unction.
examples.professional: Hospital chaplains should know that Orthodox patients may ask for holy unction even when their illness is not life-threatening.
examples.analytical: Holy unction joins healing and forgiveness, treating sickness not merely as a medical problem but as part of humanity's fallen condition.

nuance.etymology: Latin unctio “anointing,” from ungere “to anoint.”
common_mistakes: Calling it “last rites” in an Orthodox context.
Using “unction” alone, which can sound like the negative sense of exaggerated piety.
nuance.biblical_note: James 5:14-15 tells the sick to call the elders of the church to pray over them and anoint them with oil in the Lord's name, promising that the prayer of faith will save the sick and that their sins will be forgiven. In Mark 6:13 the Twelve anoint many sick people with oil and heal them.

traditions.view: Holy unction is a holy mystery for anyone suffering in body or soul, not only the dying; it is often given to the whole congregation on Holy Wednesday.
The Anointing of the Sick is a sacrament for those seriously ill or weakened by age; before Vatican II it was called extreme unction and was mostly given near death.
Generally not considered a sacrament; Anglicans and some Lutherans have rites of anointing, and Pentecostal and charismatic churches often anoint with oil in healing prayer.

senses: The week before Pascha, commemorating Christ's entry into Jerusalem, Passion, death and burial; for Orthodox, Great and Holy Week.

etymology: English translation of Latin Hebdomada Sancta and Greek Megalē Hebdomas.

core.definition: The week before Pascha, commemorating Christ's entry into Jerusalem, Passion, death and burial; for Orthodox, Great and Holy Week.

pronunciation.tip: Stress both words, with a slightly stronger stress on WEEK.

nuance.usage_note: In Byzantine practice Holy Week begins on the evening of Palm Sunday. Monday through Wednesday have the Bridegroom Matins (usually served the evening before), Holy Wednesday often has holy unction, and Thursday through Saturday commemorate the Supper, Passion, burial and descent into Hades. Greek Megalē Hebdomas; Slavonic Strastnaya sedmitsa, “Passion Week.” In the West Holy Week runs from Palm Sunday to Holy Saturday, ending with the Easter Vigil.

distinctions.note: Passion Week is another name for Holy Week, though older Western usage applied it to the week before.
Bright Week is the week after Pascha, a time of joy and no fasting.
Holy Week is not counted in the forty days of Great Lent; it follows them.

collocations: the Bridegroom services of Holy Week

examples.everyday: I took off work for Holy Week so I can make it to the services every evening.
examples.professional: Our Holy Week schedule includes the Bridegroom Matins on Sunday, Monday and Tuesday evenings.
examples.analytical: Holy Week compresses the whole history of salvation into eight days, so the faithful live the Passion in liturgical time.

nuance.etymology: English translation of Latin Hebdomada Sancta and Greek Megalē Hebdomas.
common_mistakes: Counting it as part of the forty days of Great Lent.
Assuming it falls on the same dates in Orthodox and Western calendars.
nuance.biblical_note: Holy Week follows the closing chapters of the Gospels: the entry into Jerusalem (Matthew 21:1-11; John 12:12-19), the anointing at Bethany (Matthew 26:6-13), the Last Supper, the Passion and the burial (Matthew 26-27; John 13-19).

senses: Reading each liturgical action as a picture of an event in Christ's life; Alexander Schmemann's critical term for this allegorical approach.

etymology: English illustrative (from Latin illustrare, "to light up, explain") + symbolism (from Greek symbolon, "token").

core.definition: Reading each liturgical action as a picture of an event in Christ's life; Alexander Schmemann's critical term for this allegorical approach.

pronunciation.tip: Americans stress LUS in "illustrative" (some say IL-us-tray-tiv); "symbolism" is stressed on SIM.

nuance.connotation: negative in Schmemann's usage: it names a distortion of the liturgy's meaning.
nuance.usage_note: Used in liturgical theology courses, especially in discussion of Schmemann. It refers to the medieval Byzantine commentary tradition in which, for example, the Little Entrance pictures Christ going out to preach. Schmemann argued that the liturgy is not a dramatic representation of the past but the Church's real entry into the Kingdom.

distinctions.note: For Schmemann, a real symbol makes present what it signifies; illustrative symbolism only depicts something absent.
Allegory is the general method of reading hidden meanings; illustrative symbolism is the liturgical form of it.
Mystagogy is the explanation of the mysteries to the baptized; it can be, but need not be, illustrative.

collocations: reduce the rite to illustrative symbolism

examples.everyday: I always thought the Little Entrance showed Jesus going out to preach, but Father called that illustrative symbolism.
examples.professional: Schmemann's critique of illustrative symbolism is central to his argument in For the Life of the World.
examples.analytical: Illustrative symbolism turns the assembly into spectators of a sacred drama, whereas the liturgy itself presents the assembly as the Church becoming what it is.

nuance.analogy: Like treating a wedding as a play about love instead of the event in which two people actually marry.
nuance.etymology: English illustrative (from Latin illustrare, "to light up, explain") + symbolism (from Greek symbolon, "token").
common_mistakes: Assuming it means any use of symbols; Schmemann defends real symbolism.
Using it as a neutral description; it is normally a critical term.

senses: The part of the Eucharistic prayer that retells the Last Supper and repeats Christ's words over the bread and cup: "Take, eat; this is my Body."

etymology: English institution (Latin institutio, "establishment"), because the narrative recounts Christ's founding of the Eucharist, + narrative.

core.definition: The part of the Eucharistic prayer that retells the Last Supper and repeats Christ's words over the bread and cup: "Take, eat; this is my Body."

pronunciation.tip: Americans say "in-stih-TOO-shun" (not "-TYOO-"); "narrative" is stressed on the first syllable.

nuance.usage_note: A standard term in liturgical studies for what Catholics also call the words of institution or the consecration. In the Byzantine anaphora it comes after the Sanctus and before the anamnesis and epiclesis; the priest says the words aloud and the people answer "Amen." Scholars use the term when discussing which moment, if any, effects the consecration.

distinctions.note: Words of institution are Christ's sayings themselves; the institution narrative is the whole account that frames them.
The epiclesis calls down the Holy Spirit on the gifts; Orthodox see it as completing the consecration.
The anamnesis is the remembrance that follows the narrative ("Remembering this saving commandment...").

collocations: the institution narrative and the epiclesis
an anaphora without an institution narrative

examples.everyday: At the institution narrative the priest's voice gets louder, and we all answer "Amen."
examples.professional: The anaphora of Addai and Mari is famous because it contains no explicit institution narrative.
examples.analytical: The Orthodox insistence on the epiclesis resists isolating the institution narrative as a single consecratory formula.

nuance.etymology: English institution (Latin institutio, "establishment"), because the narrative recounts Christ's founding of the Eucharist, + narrative.
common_mistakes: Calling it "the consecration" in an Orthodox context, which assumes a Western view of the moment of change.
Pronouncing "institution" with "tyoo"; that is British.
nuance.biblical_note: The institution narrative draws on the Last Supper accounts in Matthew 26:26-28, Mark 14:22-24 and Luke 22:19-20, and on Paul's account in 1 Corinthians 11:23-26, the earliest written version, where he says he received from the Lord what he handed on. Luke and Paul include the command "Do this in remembrance of me."

traditions.view: The words of institution are essential, but the gifts are changed through the whole anaphora, with the epiclesis, the prayer for the Holy Spirit, as its completion. Orthodox theology avoids fixing one exact instant of consecration.

The bread and wine become the Body and Blood of Christ when the priest, acting in the person of Christ, speaks the words of consecration. The epiclesis is present in the Roman Canon in implicit form and explicitly in newer Eucharistic Prayers.

Lutherans hold that Christ's words make his body and blood truly present in, with and under the bread and wine. Reformed and Anglican churches read the words as proclaiming the promise in a sacramental meal; many Baptists and other evangelicals see them as instituting a memorial ordinance.

senses: Prayers asking God's help for others: the Church, the world, rulers, the sick, travelers, the living and the departed.

etymology: Latin intercessio, "a going between," from intercedere, "to step between."

core.definition: Prayers asking God's help for others: the Church, the world, rulers, the sick, travelers, the living and the departed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SESH; the final s sounds like z. The t is often light, "in-er-SESH-unz," in fast American speech.

nuance.usage_note: In Byzantine worship the intercessions appear in the litanies and, most solemnly, in the anaphora after the epiclesis, where the priest commemorates the Theotokos and saints, the departed and the living. In Catholic and many Protestant churches "the intercessions" or "prayers of the people" usually means the prayers after the sermon. It is normal church vocabulary across denominations.

distinctions.note: Petitions are individual requests; intercessions are requests made on behalf of others.
A litany is a form with repeated responses; it often carries the intercessions.
Commemorations name specific people, as in the diptychs; they are part of the intercessions.

examples.everyday: Can you add my aunt to the intercessions this Sunday? She's in the hospital.
examples.professional: After the epiclesis, the intercessions widen the Eucharist to embrace the whole Church, living and departed.
examples.analytical: The placement of the intercessions within the anaphora shows that the Church prays for the world precisely as the Body offering Christ's sacrifice.

nuance.analogy: Like friends carrying a paralyzed man to Jesus on a mat.
nuance.etymology: Latin intercessio, "a going between," from intercedere, "to step between."
common_mistakes: Confusing intercession (praying for others) with intersection.
Using "intercede to someone"; Americans say "intercede for" someone or "intercede with" God.
nuance.biblical_note: 1 Timothy 2:1 urges that supplications, prayers, intercessions and thanksgivings be made for all men, including kings and those in authority. Romans 8:26-27 says the Spirit intercedes for the saints, and Hebrews 7:25 says Christ always lives to make intercession for those who draw near to God through him.

traditions.view: The Church prays for the living and the departed in every service, and asks the Theotokos and saints to intercede, since all are alive in Christ.
The Mass includes prayers for the living and the dead, and Catholics ask the intercession of Mary and the saints; prayers for the dead are linked to the doctrine of purgatory.

Protestants pray for one another and for the world, but most do not pray for the departed or ask saints in heaven to intercede, holding that Christ is the one mediator. Some Anglicans and Lutherans keep forms of commemoration of the dead.

senses: An irmos sung at the end of an ode of the Matins canon, traditionally when both choirs came down to the center of the church to sing together.

etymology: Greek katabasia, from katabainein, "to go down," because the choirs came down from their stalls.

core.definition: An irmos sung at the end of an ode of the Matins canon, traditionally when both choirs came down to the center of the church to sing together.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SEE; Americans often flap the t ("kah-duh-vuh-SEE-uh"). The plural is katavasiai or simply katavasias.

nuance.usage_note: Used by Orthodox chanters and choir directors. Seasonal katavasias are fixed for periods of the year, such as the Christmas irmoi ("Christ is born, give glory") sung in the weeks before Nativity. In many American parishes, where the canon is shortened, the katavasia may be almost all that is sung of each ode.

distinctions.note: The irmos opens an ode; the katavasia is an irmos sung at the close of the ode.
Troparia make up the body of each ode; the katavasia ends it.

examples.everyday: Starting next week we switch to the Christmas katavasia, so practice "Christ is born."
examples.professional: The rubrics specify which katavasia is sung after each ode according to the season.
examples.analytical: The katavasia preserves a trace of the cathedral rite, in which the two choirs physically descended to sing together.

nuance.etymology: Greek katabasia, from katabainein, "to go down," because the choirs came down from their stalls.
common_mistakes: Using it as a synonym for any irmos.
Spelling it catavasia; the k spelling is standard.

senses: The hymns of praise and mourning sung around Christ's tomb (the epitaphios) at Holy Saturday Matins, in three stanzas interwoven with Psalm 119 verses.

etymology: Latin lamentatio, "wailing," from lamentari, "to lament"; translates Greek Enkōmia, "praises."

core.definition: The hymns of praise and mourning sung around Christ's tomb (the epitaphios) at Holy Saturday Matins, in three stanzas interwoven with Psalm 119 verses.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TAY; the final s sounds like z.

nuance.connotation: positive and solemn: mourning filled with the hope of resurrection.
nuance.usage_note: American Orthodox parishes usually sing the Lamentations on the evening of Holy Friday, at the Matins of Holy Saturday. They are also called the Praises or, in Greek, the Enkomia; the first stasis begins in Greek "Hē zōē en taphō" ("Life in the tomb"). Do not confuse them with the Old Testament book of Lamentations, which is a different thing.

distinctions.note: The biblical book mourns the fall of Jerusalem; the Holy Saturday Lamentations mourn and praise the buried Christ.
The epitaphios is the embroidered icon of Christ's burial around which the Lamentations are sung.
The Stabat Mater is a Latin hymn on Mary at the cross, used in Western devotion.

collocations: the three stases of the Lamentations

examples.everyday: We're bringing flowers for the tomb before the Lamentations on Friday night.
examples.professional: The Lamentations are troparia inserted between the verses of Psalm 118 (119), the psalm of the departed.
examples.analytical: In the Lamentations, grief at the burial of the Creator is already shot through with Paschal light, so that mourning becomes praise.

nuance.analogy: Like a funeral that is quietly turning into a wedding feast.
nuance.etymology: Latin lamentatio, "wailing," from lamentari, "to lament"; translates Greek Enkōmia, "praises."
common_mistakes: Confusing the service hymns with the biblical Book of Lamentations.
Saying they are sung on Saturday night; they belong to the Matins served Friday evening, while Saturday night is the Paschal vigil.

senses: The evening psalms of Vespers beginning "Lord, I call upon thee" (Psalms 140, 141, 129, 116 in the Greek numbering), sung as lamps are lit and incense offered.

etymology: English lamp-lighting, translating Greek lychnikon (from lychnos, "lamp"), + psalms.

core.definition: The evening psalms of Vespers beginning "Lord, I call upon thee" (Psalms 140, 141, 129, 116 in the Greek numbering), sung as lamps are lit and incense offered.

pronunciation.tip: The p in "psalms" is silent and so is the l: say "sahmz."

nuance.connotation: neutral, with a warm sense of evening worship.
nuance.usage_note: A liturgist's term for the core of Byzantine Vespers, also called "Lord, I have cried" (Greek Kyrie ekekraxa). The stichera of the day are sung between their last verses, and the deacon censes the church. The custom goes back to the ancient lamp-lighting (lychnikon) at evening prayer.

distinctions.note: Phos Hilaron ("O Gladsome Light") is the ancient hymn sung after the lamp-lighting psalms, at the entrance.
The opening psalm of Vespers, during which the priest reads the lamp-lighting prayers, is a different element.
Stichera are the hymns of the day inserted among the verses of these psalms.

examples.everyday: My favorite part of Vespers is the lamp-lighting psalms, when the deacon goes around with the censer.
examples.professional: The lamp-lighting psalms belong to the cathedral evening office that the Typikon later combined with monastic psalmody.
examples.analytical: The lamp-lighting psalms turn the ordinary act of lighting lamps at dusk into a confession of Christ as the light that no evening can extinguish.

nuance.etymology: English lamp-lighting, translating Greek lychnikon (from lychnos, "lamp"), + psalms.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the p or l in "psalms."
Mixing Greek and Hebrew psalm numbers without saying which you use.
nuance.biblical_note: Psalm 141:2 (Hebrew numbering; Psalm 140 in the Greek), "Let my prayer be counted as incense before thee, and the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice," explains why incense is offered at this point. Psalm 130 (129 in Greek) is the cry "Out of the depths" for mercy, and Psalm 117 (116) calls all nations to praise the Lord.

senses: Greek "public work": the Church's common service of worship, in which the people of God together offer praise and become the Body of Christ.

etymology: Greek leitourgia, "public service," from leitos, "of the people," + ergon, "work."

core.definition: Greek "public work": the Church's common service of worship, in which the people of God together offer praise and become the Body of Christ.

pronunciation.tip: Stress GEE, with a hard g; modern Greek speakers say "lee-toor-YEE-ah."

nuance.usage_note: Used in liturgical theology, especially following Schmemann, to stress that liturgy is a corporate action, not a private devotion or performance by clergy. In ancient Athens a leitourgia was a public service paid for by a wealthy citizen. Today the Greek word often appears to explain the origin of English "liturgy."

distinctions.note: Latreia is worship due to God; leitourgia is the public ministry or service, including worship.
Liturgy in English often means a fixed text or service; leitourgia stresses the action of the whole people.
Devotions are private or semi-private prayers; leitourgia is the Church's official corporate act.

collocations: leitourgia as the work of the people

examples.everyday: Father reminded us that leitourgia means we all serve, not just the choir and the priest.
examples.professional: Schmemann insists that leitourgia is an action by which a group becomes something it was not as a mere collection of individuals.
examples.analytical: The civic background of leitourgia suggests that Christian worship is a public act on behalf of the world, not a retreat from it.

nuance.analogy: Like a community barn-raising: everyone has a part, and the work belongs to all.
nuance.etymology: Greek leitourgia, "public service," from leitos, "of the people," + ergon, "work."
common_mistakes: Repeating the popular claim that it literally means "work of the people" without nuance; it meant a public work done for the people.
Using a soft g in English.
nuance.biblical_note: In Luke 1:23 Zechariah goes home when his time of service (leitourgia) in the Temple ends. Hebrews 8:6 says Christ has obtained a ministry (leitourgia) much more excellent than the old one, and in Romans 15:16 Paul calls himself a minister (leitourgos) of Christ Jesus to the Gentiles in the priestly service of the gospel.

senses: Latin for "the law of belief": the Church's doctrine or rule of faith, discussed in relation to its worship (lex orandi).

etymology: Latin lex, "law," + credendi, "of believing," from credere, "to believe."

core.definition: Latin for "the law of belief": the Church's doctrine or rule of faith, discussed in relation to its worship (lex orandi).

pronunciation.tip: Stress DEN; in church Latin the c is hard, like k.

nuance.usage_note: A Latin phrase used in theology and liturgical studies, almost always together with lex orandi. It names creeds, dogmas and doctrinal teaching. Speakers use it when discussing whether worship shapes belief or belief should govern worship.

distinctions.note: Lex orandi is the law of prayer, the Church's worship; lex credendi is the law of belief.
Lex vivendi, the law of living, is a modern addition referring to Christian ethics and life.
Regula fidei, the rule of faith, is the early Church's summary of apostolic teaching.

collocations: the lex credendi of the Church

examples.everyday: Our professor kept saying lex credendi, so I finally looked it up: it just means what the Church believes.
examples.professional: The relation between lex orandi and lex credendi is central to modern liturgical theology.
examples.analytical: If lex credendi is derived from worship, doctrinal development must be traced through liturgical history as much as through conciliar texts.

nuance.etymology: Latin lex, "law," + credendi, "of believing," from credere, "to believe."
common_mistakes: Pronouncing the c as s.
Using it without its pair lex orandi.

senses: Latin for "the law of prayer": the Church's worship and liturgical practice, seen as a norm and source of its faith.

etymology: Latin lex, "law," + orandi, "of praying," from orare, "to pray."

core.definition: Latin for "the law of prayer": the Church's worship and liturgical practice, seen as a norm and source of its faith.

pronunciation.tip: Stress RAHN; the o at the start is clear, "oh," not "uh."

nuance.usage_note: A Latin phrase common in liturgical theology, Catholic, Orthodox and Anglican. It means the actual texts, rites and practice of worship, especially as evidence for doctrine. Speakers often say "the lex orandi of the Church" or argue that a reform changes the lex orandi.

distinctions.note: Lex credendi is the law of belief, the content of faith.
Rubrics are the instructions for performing worship; lex orandi is worship as a theological norm.
Liturgy is the worship itself; lex orandi names it as a rule for faith.

collocations: the lex orandi of the Church

examples.everyday: Father says if you want to know what we believe, look at the lex orandi: listen to the hymns.
examples.professional: Debates over the new Roman Missal turned in part on whether it expresses the same lex orandi as the old one.
examples.analytical: Treating the lex orandi as a theological source requires a critical account of which liturgical texts count as normative.

nuance.etymology: Latin lex, "law," + orandi, "of praying," from orare, "to pray."
common_mistakes: Pronouncing it "lex OR-and-eye."
Thinking it refers only to private prayer.

senses: "The law of prayer is the law of belief": the principle that the Church's worship expresses and shapes its faith, so liturgy is a source of theology.

etymology: Latin, "law of praying, law of believing," condensed from Prosper of Aquitaine.

core.definition: "The law of prayer is the law of belief": the principle that the Church's worship expresses and shapes its faith, so liturgy is a source of theology.

pronunciation.tip: Pause slightly at the comma; stress RAHN and DEN.

nuance.usage_note: A short form of a fifth-century saying of Prosper of Aquitaine, "ut legem credendi lex statuat supplicandi" ("that the law of supplication may establish the law of belief"). Orthodox writers use it to say that theology grows from the Church's experience in worship. Catholic teaching, as in Pius XII's Mediator Dei, also stresses that doctrine guards and judges worship.

distinctions.note: Lex orandi alone names worship; the full axiom states a relationship.

distinctions.vs: lex orandi, lex credendi, lex vivendi
distinctions.note: The three-part form adds the law of living, Christian life and ethics.

collocations: the principle lex orandi, lex credendi
the axiom lex orandi, lex credendi

examples.everyday: Our deacon loves to say "lex orandi, lex credendi": we believe what we pray.
examples.professional: This course takes lex orandi, lex credendi as its method, reading doctrine through the texts of the services.
examples.analytical: Prosper's original formula concerned the Church's intercessions as proof of the need for grace, not a general theory of liturgy and doctrine.

nuance.analogy: Like learning a family's values by watching how they eat dinner together.
nuance.etymology: Latin, "law of praying, law of believing," condensed from Prosper of Aquitaine.
common_mistakes: Attributing it to a council or to Augustine.
Translating it as "pray as you like and believe as you like."

senses: A Byzantine litany, usually after the Gospel, answered by a triple "Lord, have mercy," with petitions for the Church, clergy, nation and particular needs.

etymology: Litany from Greek litaneia, "entreaty"; fervent from Latin fervere, "to boil"; supplication from Latin supplicare, "to plead humbly."

core.definition: A Byzantine litany, usually after the Gospel, answered by a triple "Lord, have mercy," with petitions for the Church, clergy, nation and particular needs.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LIT, FUR and KAY; the t in "litany" is flapped, "LID-n-ee."

nuance.usage_note: Also called the Augmented Litany or Triple Litany; in Greek the ektenia ("intense" litany). It begins "Have mercy on us, O God, according to thy great goodness," and in many American parishes names the sick, the departed and other special needs. It occurs at Liturgy, Vespers and Matins.

distinctions.note: The Great Litany (Litany of Peace) opens the service with a single "Lord, have mercy" to each petition.
The Litany of Supplication asks "Grant this, O Lord"; it is a different litany.
A little litany is a short form between parts of a service.

examples.everyday: Father will add your grandmother's name to the Litany of Fervent Supplication on Sunday.
examples.professional: The Litany of Fervent Supplication follows the Gospel reading and homily in the Divine Liturgy.
examples.analytical: The intensity of the Litany of Fervent Supplication lies in its triple response, which turns the congregation's petition into urgent common cry.

nuance.etymology: Litany from Greek litaneia, "entreaty"; fervent from Latin fervere, "to boil"; supplication from Latin supplicare, "to plead humbly."
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the Litany of Supplication ("Grant this, O Lord").

senses: In the Divine Liturgy, the procession in which the clergy carry the Gospel book through the north door and into the altar; at Vespers, the entrance with the censer.

etymology: Translation of Greek mikra eisodos, "little entrance."

core.definition: In the Divine Liturgy, the procession in which the clergy carry the Gospel book through the north door and into the altar; at Vespers, the entrance with the censer.

pronunciation.tip: Americans flap the tt in "little" ("LID-ul"); stress EN in "entrance" (the verb en-TRANCE means something else).

nuance.usage_note: Used in Orthodox and Byzantine Catholic parishes. At the Liturgy it comes during the Third Antiphon or Beatitudes, followed by the entrance verse "Come, let us worship and fall down before Christ" and the troparia. It originally marked the entrance of clergy and people into the church at the very start of the service.

distinctions.note: The Great Entrance carries the bread and wine to the altar; the Little Entrance carries the Gospel book.
The introit is the opening chant of the Roman Mass; the Little Entrance is a procession.
At Vespers the entrance is made with the censer (or the Gospel on some feasts) during "O Gladsome Light."

collocations: the Little Entrance with the Gospel

examples.everyday: The altar boys carry candles in front of the Gospel at the Little Entrance.
examples.professional: Liturgical historians read the Little Entrance as the remnant of the bishop's entry into the church at the beginning of the Liturgy.
examples.analytical: Schmemann interprets the Little Entrance not as a picture of Christ's going out to preach but as the Church's ascent toward the throne of God.

nuance.etymology: Translation of Greek mikra eisodos, "little entrance."
common_mistakes: Confusing it with the Great Entrance.
Stressing the second syllable of "entrance."

senses: A nineteenth- and twentieth-century movement, mainly Catholic but also Protestant and Orthodox, to renew worship through historical study and active participation of the people.

etymology: English liturgical (from Greek leitourgia) + movement.

core.definition: A nineteenth- and twentieth-century movement, mainly Catholic but also Protestant and Orthodox, to renew worship through historical study and active participation of the people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TUR and MOOV.

nuance.connotation: neutral to positive, though its results are debated.
nuance.usage_note: Associated with Benedictine centers such as Solesmes, Maria Laach and, in the United States, St. John's Abbey in Collegeville, and with figures like Lambert Beauduin and Virgil Michel. It shaped Vatican II's Constitution on the Sacred Liturgy. Orthodox theologians such as Schmemann and Afanasiev engaged it and promoted a eucharistic revival, including more frequent Communion.

distinctions.note: Liturgical reform is official revision of rites; the liturgical movement was the broader scholarly and pastoral renewal that led to it.
Ressourcement is the wider return to patristic sources in twentieth-century Catholic theology.

collocations: the liturgical movement and Vatican II

examples.everyday: Our professor said the liturgical movement is why many Catholics now sing and answer at Mass.
examples.professional: Schmemann's work cannot be understood apart from his dialogue with the Western liturgical movement.
examples.analytical: The liturgical movement's ideal of active participation rested on a renewed ecclesiology of the assembly as the subject of worship.

nuance.etymology: English liturgical (from Greek leitourgia) + movement.
common_mistakes: Equating the movement with the post-Vatican II reforms alone.
Assuming it was only Catholic.

senses: The way believers experience, understand and relate to worship; for Schmemann, a piety often detached from the liturgy's real meaning.

etymology: English liturgical + piety (Latin pietas, "dutiful devotion").

core.definition: The way believers experience, understand and relate to worship; for Schmemann, a piety often detached from the liturgy's real meaning.

pronunciation.tip: Stress PY in "piety"; the t is often flapped, "PY-uh-dee."

nuance.connotation: neutral; often critical in Schmemann's analysis.
nuance.usage_note: A key term in Schmemann's Introduction to Liturgical Theology, where he argues that the forms of worship remained traditional while the way people perceived them changed. For example, the Eucharist came to be experienced as an object of private devotion rather than the action of the gathered Church. Others use the phrase positively for a spirituality nourished by the liturgy.

distinctions.note: Lex orandi is worship as norm; liturgical piety is the believer's subjective relation to it.
Devotionalism is private devotions displacing the liturgy, one form of distorted liturgical piety.
Liturgical theology studies worship's meaning; liturgical piety is how it is lived and felt.

examples.everyday: Our priest said that coming only to watch, not to commune, is a problem of liturgical piety.
examples.professional: Schmemann distinguishes the unchanged order of worship from the liturgical piety that interprets it.
examples.analytical: A change in liturgical piety can transform the meaning of a rite even when not a single word of the text has changed.

nuance.analogy: Like a piece of music played perfectly but heard by an audience that no longer understands what it means.
nuance.etymology: English liturgical + piety (Latin pietas, "dutiful devotion").
common_mistakes: Using it only as praise; in Schmemann it is often a diagnostic term.

senses: Official revision of a church's rites, texts or service books, such as Patriarch Nikon's reforms in Russia or the Catholic reform after Vatican II.

etymology: Liturgical (Greek leitourgia) + reform (Latin reformare, "to shape again").

core.definition: Official revision of a church's rites, texts or service books, such as Patriarch Nikon's reforms in Russia or the Catholic reform after Vatican II.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TUR and FORM.

nuance.connotation: neutral, but often controversial in practice.
nuance.usage_note: Used in historical and theological discussion. In Orthodoxy the most famous case is the seventeenth-century reform under Patriarch Nikon, which led to the Old Believer schism; Orthodox churches are generally cautious about reform. In Catholicism it usually means the revision ordered by Vatican II, including the Missal of Paul VI.

distinctions.note: The liturgical movement was scholarly and pastoral renewal; liturgical reform is the official change of texts and rites.
Renewal can mean deeper understanding without changing texts.
The Reformation was the sixteenth-century Protestant break, broader than liturgy.

examples.everyday: My Russian grandmother still talks about the Old Believers and the old liturgical reform that split the Church.
examples.professional: Any liturgical reform must ask whether it restores the meaning of the rite or merely adjusts its form.
examples.analytical: Schmemann warned that liturgical reform without a recovery of liturgical theology would only change externals.

nuance.etymology: Liturgical (Greek leitourgia) + reform (Latin reformare, "to shape again").
common_mistakes: Assuming liturgical reform always means simplification.

senses: Time as sanctified by the Church's worship, in which past saving events and the coming Kingdom become present in the rhythm of services and feasts.

etymology: Liturgical (Greek leitourgia) + time (Old English tima).

core.definition: Time as sanctified by the Church's worship, in which past saving events and the coming Kingdom become present in the rhythm of services and feasts.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TUR in "liturgical."

nuance.usage_note: A theme of liturgical theology, especially in Schmemann, who speaks of the liturgy of time: the daily, weekly and yearly cycles that sanctify time while pointing beyond it to the eighth day. The hymns' constant "today" ("Today Christ is born") expresses this sense. Scholars contrast it with ordinary chronological time.

distinctions.note: Kairos is the decisive, God-given moment; liturgical time is the whole ordered pattern in which such moments are celebrated.
Chronos is clock time; liturgical time transforms it.
The liturgical cycle is the structure; liturgical time is its theological meaning.

examples.everyday: When we sing "Today he who hung the earth upon the waters is hung on the cross," it feels like liturgical time collapses the centuries.
examples.professional: Schmemann argues that liturgical time is eschatological: it sanctifies this world's time by referring it to the Kingdom.
examples.analytical: Liturgical time is neither cyclical myth nor mere commemoration, but the presence of a once-for-all event within the repetitions of the year.

nuance.analogy: Like a window in the wall of the calendar that opens onto eternity.
nuance.etymology: Liturgical (Greek leitourgia) + time (Old English tima).
common_mistakes: Treating it as just the dates of feasts.

senses: Christian witness, mission and service to the world that flow out of the Eucharist, continuing the Liturgy in daily life.

etymology: English phrase from twentieth-century Orthodox mission theology.

core.definition: Christian witness, mission and service to the world that flow out of the Eucharist, continuing the Liturgy in daily life.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LIT in both "liturgy"s; the t is flapped, "LID-er-jee."

nuance.usage_note: A phrase associated with Orthodox mission theology, especially Archbishop Anastasios of Albania and the Romanian theologian Ion Bria. It is now common in American Orthodox preaching about service, outreach and evangelism. The dismissal "Let us go forth in peace" is often cited as its starting point.

distinctions.note: The social gospel focuses on social reform; the liturgy after the liturgy roots service in the Eucharist.
Diakonia is service in general; the phrase stresses its eucharistic source.
Mission is broader; the phrase names mission as an extension of worship.

collocations: live the liturgy after the liturgy
the liturgy after the liturgy and mission

examples.everyday: Serving at the soup kitchen after church is our parish's liturgy after the liturgy.
examples.professional: The homily presented the liturgy after the liturgy as the natural outcome of receiving Communion.
examples.analytical: The idea of the liturgy after the liturgy overcomes the split between worship and ethics by making the world the place where the Eucharist continues.

nuance.analogy: Like a river that keeps flowing after leaving its source.
nuance.etymology: English phrase from twentieth-century Orthodox mission theology.
common_mistakes: Thinking it refers to a second service or coffee hour.

senses: The longer Byzantine Eucharistic Liturgy, with an anaphora attributed to St. Basil the Great, served about ten times a year, including Lenten Sundays.

etymology: Named for St. Basil the Great (died 379), archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to whom the anaphora is attributed.

core.definition: The longer Byzantine Eucharistic Liturgy, with an anaphora attributed to St. Basil the Great, served about ten times a year, including Lenten Sundays.

pronunciation.tip: Americans say "BAZ-ul" for the saint; Greek speakers say "vah-SEE-lee-os." "St." is read "saint."

nuance.usage_note: It is served on the first five Sundays of Great Lent, Holy Thursday, Holy Saturday, the eves of Nativity and Theophany (or the feasts themselves in some years) and on St. Basil's day, January 1. Its structure matches the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, but the priest's prayers, above all the anaphora, are longer and richer in biblical theology. Parishioners notice it mainly because the Communion hymn time is longer and "All of creation rejoices in thee" replaces "It is truly meet."

distinctions.note: The Chrysostom Liturgy is the usual one; the Basil Liturgy is longer and used about ten times a year.
The Presanctified is not a full Eucharist and has no anaphora.
The Liturgy of St. James is an ancient Jerusalem rite, served rarely today.

collocations: serve the Liturgy of St. Basil
All of creation rejoices in thee

examples.everyday: Plan for church to run a little longer on Sunday; it's the Liturgy of St. Basil.
examples.professional: The anaphora of the Liturgy of St. Basil offers a full narration of salvation history from creation to the Second Coming.
examples.analytical: The Liturgy of St. Basil shows how fourth-century Trinitarian theology was absorbed into the Church's eucharistic prayer.

nuance.etymology: Named for St. Basil the Great (died 379), archbishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, to whom the anaphora is attributed.
common_mistakes: Thinking it is a different order of service; only the priest's prayers and a few hymns differ.
Confusing St. Basil the Great with St. Basil the Blessed of Moscow.

senses: The ordinary Eucharistic Liturgy of the Byzantine rite, served on most Sundays and weekdays, with an anaphora attributed to St. John Chrysostom.

etymology: Named for St. John Chrysostom (died 407), archbishop of Constantinople; Chrysostom is Greek for "golden-mouthed."

core.definition: The ordinary Eucharistic Liturgy of the Byzantine rite, served on most Sundays and weekdays, with an anaphora attributed to St. John Chrysostom.

pronunciation.tip: Americans most often say "KRIS-us-tum"; "kris-AHS-tum" is also common. The ch is a k sound.

nuance.usage_note: This is "the Divine Liturgy" Orthodox Christians attend almost every Sunday, in Greek, Slavonic, English, Arabic and many other languages. Its anaphora is shorter than St. Basil's; scholars debate how much of it goes back to Chrysostom himself. Orthodox people usually just say "the Liturgy" or "Divine Liturgy."

distinctions.note: The Basil Liturgy has the same structure but longer prayers and is used about ten times a year.
Mass is the Western term for the Eucharist; Orthodox say Divine Liturgy.
Divine Liturgy is the general name; the Chrysostom Liturgy is its most common form.

collocations: the Divine Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom
serve the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom
a setting of the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom

examples.everyday: Most Sundays we have the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, and it's over by noon.
examples.professional: Rachmaninoff and Tchaikovsky both composed choral settings of the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom.
examples.analytical: The Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom reached its present form through centuries of development, so its name indicates the anaphora's traditional attribution rather than a single author.

nuance.etymology: Named for St. John Chrysostom (died 407), archbishop of Constantinople; Chrysostom is Greek for "golden-mouthed."
common_mistakes: Assuming Chrysostom wrote every word of the service.
Calling it "the Chrysostom Mass."

senses: The first part of the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, with litanies, antiphons, the Little Entrance and the Scripture readings, once open to those preparing for baptism.

etymology: Catechumen from Greek katēchoumenos, "one being instructed," from katēchein, "to teach by word of mouth."

core.definition: The first part of the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, with litanies, antiphons, the Little Entrance and the Scripture readings, once open to those preparing for baptism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress KYOO in "catechumens"; the ch is a k sound, and the t is often flapped.

nuance.usage_note: The name comes from the ancient practice of letting catechumens (people preparing for baptism) attend only this part. It ends with the litany for the catechumens and the call "All catechumens, depart," which is still said in many parishes even though catechumens usually stay. The Roman equivalent is the Liturgy of the Word.

distinctions.note: The Liturgy of the Faithful follows and centers on the Eucharist.
The Liturgy of the Word is the Roman name for the corresponding part of the Mass.
The Proskomedia, the preparation of the gifts, takes place before this part begins.

collocations: during the Liturgy of the Catechumens

examples.everyday: As a catechumen, I used to step out after the Liturgy of the Catechumens, but our priest now asks us to stay and pray.
examples.professional: The Liturgy of the Catechumens culminates in the reading of the Gospel and the homily.
examples.analytical: The division between the Liturgy of the Catechumens and the Liturgy of the Faithful embodies an ecclesiology in which the Eucharist belongs to the baptized assembly.

nuance.etymology: Catechumen from Greek katēchoumenos, "one being instructed," from katēchein, "to teach by word of mouth."
common_mistakes: Pronouncing catechumens with a ch as in "church."
Thinking catechumens must always leave today; practice varies.

senses: The second part of the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, for the baptized: the Great Entrance, Creed, anaphora and Holy Communion.

etymology: Faithful from Middle English feithful, "full of faith"; here it means the baptized members of the Church.

core.definition: The second part of the Byzantine Divine Liturgy, for the baptized: the Great Entrance, Creed, anaphora and Holy Communion.

pronunciation.tip: Stress FAYTH; the th is unvoiced, as in "think."

nuance.usage_note: It begins after the dismissal of the catechumens with the litanies of the faithful and runs through the Great Entrance, kiss of peace, Creed, anaphora, Communion and dismissal. The Roman equivalent is the Liturgy of the Eucharist. Liturgists use the name to stress that the Eucharist is the act of the whole baptized assembly.

distinctions.note: The Liturgy of the Catechumens comes first and centers on the readings.
The Liturgy of the Eucharist is the Roman Catholic name for the corresponding part of the Mass.
The anaphora is the eucharistic prayer, the heart of the Liturgy of the Faithful.

collocations: the Great Entrance begins the Liturgy of the Faithful

examples.everyday: Once I was baptized, the Liturgy of the Faithful felt different, because now I could receive Communion.
examples.professional: The deacon's "The doors! The doors!" before the Creed recalls the closing of the church during the Liturgy of the Faithful.
examples.analytical: In the Liturgy of the Faithful the assembly acts as the royal priesthood, offering the gifts with and through the presiding bishop or priest.

nuance.etymology: Faithful from Middle English feithful, "full of faith"; here it means the baptized members of the Church.
common_mistakes: Thinking only clergy take part; the whole baptized assembly participates.

senses: A Lenten evening service of Vespers with Holy Communion from Gifts consecrated at a previous Sunday Liturgy, served on weekdays when no full Liturgy is allowed.

etymology: Presanctified, from Latin prae-, "before," + sanctificare, "to make holy": Gifts made holy beforehand.

core.definition: A Lenten evening service of Vespers with Holy Communion from Gifts consecrated at a previous Sunday Liturgy, served on weekdays when no full Liturgy is allowed.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SANGK in "Presanctified"; the n before c sounds like "ng," so say "SANGK-tuh."

nuance.connotation: positive: a beloved, solemn Lenten service.
nuance.usage_note: Served on Wednesdays and Fridays of Great Lent (and sometimes other weekdays) and on the first three days of Holy Week, since the full Eucharist is not celebrated on Lenten weekdays. It is traditionally attributed to St. Gregory the Dialogist (Pope Gregory the Great). Parishes often serve it in the evening, and the faithful keep a strict fast before it; people often just say "Presanctified."

distinctions.note: The Divine Liturgy has an anaphora that consecrates the Gifts; the Presanctified has none.
The Roman Good Friday service also gives Communion from Hosts consecrated earlier, historically called the Mass of the Presanctified.
A Vesperal Liturgy is a full Liturgy of St. Basil or Chrysostom joined to Vespers.

collocations: the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts in Holy Week

examples.everyday: Are you coming to Presanctified on Wednesday night? We're having a Lenten potluck after.
examples.professional: In the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, the Gifts are transferred to the altar in silence, as the choir sings "Now the powers of heaven."
examples.analytical: The Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts reveals a tension between the Lenten restriction on the Eucharist and the Church's desire for frequent Communion.

nuance.analogy: Like eating from bread baked on Sunday to keep you strong through the week's fast.
nuance.etymology: Presanctified, from Latin prae-, "before," + sanctificare, "to make holy": Gifts made holy beforehand.
common_mistakes: Calling it a "Mass" or saying the Gifts are consecrated during it.
Pronouncing "Presanctified" with the stress on "pre."
nuance.biblical_note: Psalm 141:2, "Let my prayer be counted as incense before thee, and the lifting up of my hands as an evening sacrifice," is sung with great solemnity in this service, while the priest censes the altar.

senses: The part of a Eucharistic service centered on Scripture readings and preaching; mainly the Roman Catholic name, corresponding to the Byzantine Liturgy of the Catechumens.

etymology: Liturgy (Greek leitourgia, "public service") + Word, meaning the Word of God in Scripture.

core.definition: The part of a Eucharistic service centered on Scripture readings and preaching; mainly the Roman Catholic name, corresponding to the Byzantine Liturgy of the Catechumens.

pronunciation.tip: "Word" has the r-colored vowel of "bird"; the t in "liturgy" is flapped.

nuance.usage_note: Catholics in the US hear this term constantly: readings from the Old Testament, a psalm, an epistle and the Gospel, then the homily, Creed and Prayer of the Faithful. Lutherans, Anglicans and Methodists use similar language. Orthodox speakers usually say "Liturgy of the Catechumens" or "Liturgy of the Word" when explaining their service to others.

distinctions.note: The Byzantine name for the corresponding part of the Divine Liturgy.
The Liturgy of the Eucharist follows the Liturgy of the Word in the Roman Mass.
A service of the Word can be a standalone service without Communion, common in Protestant churches.

collocations: during the Liturgy of the Word
Liturgy of the Word with children
the homily and the Liturgy of the Word

examples.everyday: The kids go downstairs for their own Liturgy of the Word and come back for Communion.
examples.professional: Vatican II expanded the lectionary so that the Liturgy of the Word would offer the faithful a richer share of Scripture.
examples.analytical: Calling it the Liturgy of the Word presents Scripture reading itself as an act of worship, not merely instruction preceding the sacrament.

nuance.etymology: Liturgy (Greek leitourgia, "public service") + Word, meaning the Word of God in Scripture.
common_mistakes: Using it as if it were the standard Orthodox name; Orthodox service books say Liturgy of the Catechumens.
nuance.biblical_note: Luke 4:16-21 shows Jesus reading Isaiah in the synagogue at Nazareth and saying the Scripture is fulfilled today, an early model of reading and preaching in worship. Nehemiah 8:1-8 describes Ezra reading the law to the people and giving the sense, and Luke 24:27 shows Christ interpreting the Scriptures to the disciples on the road to Emmaus before breaking bread.

senses: The Church's daily, weekly and yearly cycles of services, such as Vespers, Matins and the feasts, through which time itself is sanctified.

etymology: Liturgy from Greek leitourgia, 'public work or service'; the phrase is a modern term of liturgical theology.

core.definition: The Church's daily, weekly and yearly cycles of services, such as Vespers, Matins and the feasts, through which time itself is sanctified.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LIT in liturgy and say the middle vowel as a quick 'er'; 'of' reduces to 'uv' and links to 'time'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in Orthodox writing it is positive, describing time as a gift offered back to God.
nuance.usage_note: A term of liturgical theology, used above all since Alexander Schmemann, who contrasted the liturgy of time (the hours, the week centered on Sunday, the church year) with the Eucharist that fulfills it. You will meet it in seminary courses and books, rarely in parish talk, where people say 'the daily services' or 'the church calendar'.

distinctions.note: The Roman Catholic name for the daily office alone; the liturgy of time also includes the weekly and yearly cycles.
The yearly cycle of feasts and fasts only, one part of the liturgy of time.
The Eucharistic service itself, which the liturgy of time surrounds and points toward.

examples.everyday: Our priest says Vespers on Saturday night is part of the liturgy of time, not just a warm-up for Sunday.
examples.professional: This week's seminar looks at how Schmemann relates the liturgy of time to the Eucharist.
examples.analytical: In the liturgy of time the Church does not escape history but transforms its hours, days and seasons into a movement toward the Kingdom.

nuance.analogy: Like a frame of hours, days and seasons set around the Eucharist, the picture at its center.
nuance.etymology: Liturgy from Greek leitourgia, 'public work or service'; the phrase is a modern term of liturgical theology.
common_mistakes: Using it to mean only the church calendar of feasts, leaving out the daily services.
Writing 'liturgy of the time'; the set phrase has no second 'the'.
nuance.biblical_note: The daily rhythm of prayer echoes Psalm 119:164, where the psalmist praises God seven times a day, and Psalm 119:62, rising at midnight to give thanks; these verses shaped the Church's cycle of hours.

senses: In Orthodox ecclesiology, the whole Church fully present in one Eucharistic community gathered around its bishop, not a mere branch of a larger body.

etymology: Local from Latin localis, 'of a place'; church from Greek kyriakon, 'the Lord's (house)'.

core.definition: In Orthodox ecclesiology, the whole Church fully present in one Eucharistic community gathered around its bishop, not a mere branch of a larger body.

pronunciation.tip: Both words carry stress; the 'l' at the end of local is dark, like in 'full', and church has one r-colored vowel: 'CHERCH'.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; in theology it carries a strong, positive sense of fullness rather than smallness.
nuance.usage_note: In everyday American speech 'my local church' just means the congregation near my home. In Orthodox theology (Afanasiev, Zizioulas) it is a technical term: the diocese, the people with their bishop celebrating the Eucharist, which is the Catholic Church in that place. Context tells you which meaning is intended.

distinctions.note: A parish is a community led by a priest under a bishop; in strict Orthodox usage the local church is the bishop's diocese.
The Church throughout the world; Orthodox eucharistic ecclesiology sees it as the communion of local churches, not a sum of parts.
A self-governing church such as the Church of Serbia, sometimes also called a local church in a broader, national sense.

collocations: the bishop and his local church
eucharistic ecclesiology of the local church

examples.everyday: Father explained that our diocese isn't a piece of the Church; it's the local church, the whole Church right here.
examples.professional: Zizioulas argues that the local church is catholic because the whole Christ is present in its Eucharist.
examples.analytical: Eucharistic ecclesiology locates catholicity in the local church gathered around its bishop rather than in a universal administrative center.

nuance.analogy: Like a hologram: each piece contains the whole picture, not a fragment of it.
nuance.etymology: Local from Latin localis, 'of a place'; church from Greek kyriakon, 'the Lord's (house)'.
common_mistakes: Assuming it means a small or minor congregation; in theology it means the Church in its fullness.
Equating it with a parish when the author means the bishop's diocese.
nuance.biblical_note: Paul addresses 'the church of God which is at Corinth' (1 Corinthians 1:2), the whole Church present in one city, a key text for the theology of the local church.

traditions.view: The local church, the diocese gathered around its bishop in the Eucharist, is the Catholic Church in that place; the universal Church is the communion of local churches.

The particular church (diocese) is truly the Church, but it is fully catholic only in communion with the bishop of Rome; Catholic theology stresses that the universal Church is not just a federation of local ones.

Many Protestants, especially Baptists and Congregationalists, see the local congregation of believers as the basic church; Anglicans and Lutherans with bishops often think in terms of dioceses or national churches.

senses: The ancient evening rite of lighting the lamps at sunset with thanksgiving to Christ the light; its core survives in Byzantine Vespers.

etymology: Latin lucernarium, from lucerna, 'lamp'; Greek equivalent lychnikon.

core.definition: The ancient evening rite of lighting the lamps at sunset with thanksgiving to Christ the light; its core survives in Byzantine Vespers.

pronunciation.tip: Stress NAIR. The c is soft (s) in American Latin; some liturgists say 'loo-chair-NAH-ree-um' in the Italian style.

nuance.usage_note: A liturgical history term heard in seminary courses and scholarly writing. In Byzantine Vespers its descendants are the evening psalms 'Lord, I call upon thee' (Psalm 141 and others), the entrance with the censer, and the ancient hymn 'O Gladsome Light' (Phos hilaron). In the West the term also describes the light service at the start of the Easter Vigil.

distinctions.note: Vespers is the full evening office; the lucernarium is its ancient lamp-lighting core.
The hymn sung at the lamp-lighting, not the rite itself.
