A stavrosimon (staurosimon) is a hymn of the Cross that does not center on the Theotokos.
The Stabat Mater is a Latin medieval hymn on the same theme, from a different tradition.

examples.everyday: Our chanter explained that the hymn about Mary weeping at the Cross is called a staurotheotokion.
examples.professional: On Friday evening, the staurotheotokion replaces the usual theotokion at Vespers.
examples.analytical: The staurotheotokia interpret the Passion through the Mother's compassion, linking Simeon's prophecy of the sword to the Cross.

nuance.analogy: Like a lament sung by a mother at her son's side, set into the Church's daily prayer.
nuance.etymology: Greek stavros (cross) + Theotokos (God-bearer) + -ion (diminutive, a hymn).
common_mistakes: Spelling it staurotheotokon.
Confusing it with the Western Stabat Mater.
nuance.biblical_note: The hymns draw on John 19:25-27, where Mary stands by the Cross and Jesus entrusts her to the beloved disciple, and on Simeon's prophecy that a sword will pierce through her own soul (Luke 2:35).

senses: The liturgical and monastic rule of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, shaped by St. Theodore the Studite, dominant before the Sabaite Typikon.

etymology: Studite from Stoudios, founder of the monastery; Typikon from Greek typikon, from typos, pattern.

core.definition: The liturgical and monastic rule of the Stoudios monastery in Constantinople, shaped by St. Theodore the Studite, dominant before the Sabaite Typikon.

pronunciation.tip: Studite is STOO-dyte, stress on the first syllable; the t in -dite is light.

nuance.usage_note: A term of liturgical history. St. Theodore the Studite (759-826) organized cenobitic life at Stoudios, and the Studite synthesis combined Palestinian monastic offices with Constantinopolitan usage. It spread to Athos and to Kievan Rus', where the Kiev Caves monastery adopted it, before the Sabaite Typikon replaced it.

distinctions.note: The Sabaite (Jerusalem) Typikon replaced the Studite rule and underlies current Byzantine practice.
The cathedral rite of Hagia Sophia was the urban sung office, distinct from both monastic Typika.
The Hypotyposis is a Studite rule document, an early witness to the Studite Typikon.

examples.everyday: Our liturgy professor said the Studite Typikon is why so many Lenten hymns come from Constantinople.
examples.professional: Students should compare the Studite Typikon with the later Sabaite usage in the structure of Matins.
examples.analytical: The Studite Typikon reflects the encounter of urban and monastic liturgy after the iconoclast crisis.

nuance.analogy: Like the first edition of a rulebook that was later revised and replaced.
nuance.etymology: Studite from Stoudios, founder of the monastery; Typikon from Greek typikon, from typos, pattern.
common_mistakes: Pronouncing Studite like student, STOO-dent.
Thinking it is still the standard rule today.

senses: The first Sunday of Great Lent, celebrating the restoration of holy icons in 843 and the victory of true faith over heresy.

etymology: Translation of Greek Kyriakē tēs Orthodoxias; the feast dates from the restoration of icons in 843 under Empress Theodora.

core.definition: The first Sunday of Great Lent, celebrating the restoration of holy icons in 843 and the victory of true faith over heresy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress OR in Orthodoxy, with a lighter stress on dok; "of" shrinks to "uv."

nuance.connotation: Positive and festive; a celebration of Orthodox identity.
nuance.usage_note: Orthodox Americans use it constantly; many parishes have a pan-Orthodox Vespers that evening, and children carry icons in procession after the Liturgy. The Synodikon of Orthodoxy is read on this day in cathedrals and monasteries. It is also called the Triumph of Orthodoxy.

distinctions.note: Another name for the same feast, stressing the victory over iconoclasm.
Forgiveness Sunday is the Sunday before Lent begins; the Sunday of Orthodoxy is the first Sunday in Lent.
Several Sundays honor the Fathers of councils; the Sunday of Orthodoxy specifically celebrates the Seventh Council's teaching on icons.

collocations: pan-Orthodox Vespers on the Sunday of Orthodoxy

examples.everyday: Bring an icon from home on Sunday of Orthodoxy; the kids will carry them around the church after Liturgy.
examples.professional: This year's Sunday of Orthodoxy Vespers will be hosted at the Greek cathedral, with clergy from all jurisdictions.
examples.analytical: By linking the first Sunday of Lent to the restoration of icons in 843, the Church presents the Incarnation as the foundation of all right worship.

nuance.etymology: Translation of Greek Kyriakē tēs Orthodoxias; the feast dates from the restoration of icons in 843 under Empress Theodora.
common_mistakes: Thinking it celebrates the founding of the Orthodox Church; it marks the end of iconoclasm.
Placing it before Lent; it is the first Sunday of Lent.

senses: Latin for "Lift up your hearts": the opening dialogue of the Eucharistic prayer between priest and people.

etymology: Latin sursum "upward" + corda "hearts"; Greek anō schōmen tas kardias.

core.definition: Latin for "Lift up your hearts": the opening dialogue of the Eucharistic prayer between priest and people.

pronunciation.tip: Stress COR; many Americans also say "SER-sum." Pronounce the c as k.

nuance.connotation: Neutral; a technical name for a solemn moment.
nuance.usage_note: Used by liturgists, clergy and seminarians, mostly in writing. In the Byzantine Divine Liturgy the priest says "Let us lift up our hearts" and the people answer "We lift them up unto the Lord"; Western rites have "Lift up your hearts" and "We lift them up to the Lord." Orthodox laypeople rarely use the Latin name.

distinctions.note: The anaphora is the whole Eucharistic prayer; the Sursum corda is the dialogue that opens it.
In the Roman rite the preface is the thanksgiving that follows the Sursum corda and leads to the Sanctus.
The Sanctus ("Holy, holy, holy") comes a little later in the prayer.

examples.everyday: When the priest says "Let us lift up our hearts," that's the Sursum corda; it's one of the oldest parts of the service.
examples.professional: Notice that the Sursum corda appears in almost every ancient anaphora, East and West.
examples.analytical: The Sursum corda frames the Eucharist as an ascent: the assembly is lifted to the heavenly altar rather than bringing Christ down to earth.

nuance.etymology: Latin sursum "upward" + corda "hearts"; Greek anō schōmen tas kardias.
common_mistakes: Using it for the whole Eucharistic prayer instead of its opening dialogue.
Reading "corda" as English "cord."
nuance.biblical_note: The phrase echoes Lamentations 3:41, where the people call one another to lift up their hearts and hands to God in heaven; in the liturgy it becomes a call to set the mind on things above (compare Colossians 3:1-2).

senses: The Orthodox name for the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, sung or read at every Divine Liturgy and at baptism.

etymology: From Greek symbolon "token, sign of recognition," from symballein "to put together."

core.definition: The Orthodox name for the Nicene-Constantinopolitan Creed, sung or read at every Divine Liturgy and at baptism.

pronunciation.tip: Stress SIM and FAYTH; "of" is a weak "uv." The th in faith is soft, as in "think."

nuance.usage_note: Orthodox service books and catechisms say "the Symbol of Faith"; in conversation many Orthodox Americans just say "the Creed." It is said after the kiss of peace and the deacon's cry "The doors! The doors!" and at baptism by the candidate or sponsor. Orthodox use the text without the filioque.

distinctions.note: "Creed" is the general English word; "Symbol of Faith" is the traditional Orthodox title for this specific creed.
The Apostles' Creed is a Western baptismal creed; it is not used in Orthodox worship.
Here symbol means a token of identity or summary of faith (Greek symbolon), not a picture or sign.

collocations: the Symbol of Faith without the filioque

examples.everyday: Our godson has to learn the Symbol of Faith by heart before his baptism.
examples.professional: In catechism class we go through the Symbol of Faith one article at a time.
examples.analytical: The Symbol of Faith functions less as a theological essay than as a baptismal confession, the Church's password of identity.

nuance.analogy: Like the matching halves of a broken token that proved two people belonged together, the Symbol of Faith identifies those who share one faith.
nuance.etymology: From Greek symbolon "token, sign of recognition," from symballein "to put together."
common_mistakes: Thinking "symbol" means the creed is merely symbolic.
Confusing it with the Apostles' Creed.

traditions.view: The Creed of Nicaea (325) and Constantinople (381) is confessed in its original form, saying the Holy Spirit proceeds from the Father, without the filioque.
The Latin rite confesses the Creed with the filioque ("and the Son"), which it regards as a legitimate clarification; Eastern Catholic churches often omit it.

Lutherans, Anglicans and many Reformed and Methodist churches use the Nicene Creed with the filioque, often alongside the Apostles' Creed; many Baptist and free churches do not recite creeds in worship.

senses: "Primary theology": the Church's act of worship itself, seen as the first and basic way the Church speaks about God.

etymology: Latin, "first theology."

core.definition: "Primary theology": the Church's act of worship itself, seen as the first and basic way the Church speaks about God.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LOH and PREE; some scholars say "tay-oh-LOH-jee-ah," with a more Italian Latin sound.

nuance.usage_note: Used in academic liturgical theology, especially by the Benedictine Aidan Kavanagh and David Fagerberg, who built on Alexander Schmemann's idea that the liturgy is the Church's own theology. It is paired with theologia secunda, scholarly reflection on worship. Rarely heard outside seminaries and journals.

distinctions.note: Secondary theology reflects on worship from outside; primary theology is the worship itself.
Lex orandi, lex credendi states that the rule of prayer shapes the rule of faith; theologia prima names the liturgy as theology.
A theology of liturgy treats worship as a topic; theologia prima treats it as the source.

examples.everyday: My professor says the Liturgy itself is theologia prima; the books come second.
examples.professional: Kavanagh's distinction between theologia prima and secunda is essential for this course.
examples.analytical: To call the liturgy theologia prima is to claim that the worshiping assembly, not the academy, is the primary theologian.

nuance.analogy: Theologia prima is the music; theologia secunda is the musicology written about it.
nuance.etymology: Latin, "first theology."
common_mistakes: Taking it to mean "the most important doctrines."
Attributing the Latin phrase itself to Schmemann; it is associated with Kavanagh.

senses: "Secondary theology": scholars' reflection on and explanation of the Church's worship, which comes after the liturgy itself.

etymology: Latin, "second theology."

core.definition: "Secondary theology": scholars' reflection on and explanation of the Church's worship, which comes after the liturgy itself.

pronunciation.tip: Stress LOH and KOON; the first syllable of secunda is a weak "suh."

nuance.usage_note: A term from academic liturgical theology (Aidan Kavanagh, David Fagerberg), always paired with theologia prima. It is not an insult: secondary theology is necessary, but it depends on worship rather than the other way around.

distinctions.note: Primary theology is the act of worship; secondary theology reflects on it.
Systematic theology organizes doctrine as a whole; theologia secunda in this scheme includes all reflective theology, liturgical study among it.

collocations: theologia secunda reflects on theologia prima

examples.everyday: My thesis is theologia secunda; I'm writing about the Liturgy, not praying it.
examples.professional: Our seminar is an exercise in theologia secunda, so we must keep returning to the actual services.
examples.analytical: When theologia secunda forgets its source, it judges the liturgy by categories foreign to the liturgy.

nuance.etymology: Latin, "second theology."
common_mistakes: Thinking it means "less important theology."
Stressing the first syllable of secunda.

senses: Baptism by plunging the person fully under water three times, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

etymology: Latin triplex "threefold" + immersio "a dipping in."

core.definition: Baptism by plunging the person fully under water three times, in the name of the Father, the Son and the Holy Spirit.

pronunciation.tip: Stress TRIP and MUR; the s in immersion sounds like the s in "measure" (zh).

nuance.connotation: Neutral; for Orthodox, the proper and normal form of baptism.
nuance.usage_note: Orthodox Americans describe baptism this way, and Orthodox priests insist on it wherever possible, even for adults in a large font. Also called trine immersion. It symbolizes the Trinity and Christ's three days in the tomb.

distinctions.note: Affusion is pouring water over the head; triple immersion puts the whole body under water.
Aspersion is sprinkling.
Believer's baptism refers to who is baptized (adults who confess faith), not the number of immersions.

examples.everyday: The baby cried after the triple immersion, but the priest said that's a good sign she's alive and well.
examples.professional: The rubrics require triple immersion with the invocation of each Person of the Trinity.
examples.analytical: Triple immersion enacts the confession of the Trinity and the believer's burial and rising with Christ.

nuance.etymology: Latin triplex "threefold" + immersio "a dipping in."
common_mistakes: Saying "triple baptism"; it is one baptism with three immersions.
Thinking it is only for infants.
nuance.biblical_note: Matthew 28:19 commands baptism in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit, the basis of the three immersions. Romans 6:3-4 speaks of being buried with Christ by baptism into death, which immersion pictures. The New Testament itself does not specify three immersions; the Didache and early Fathers attest the practice.

traditions.view: Triple immersion is the norm and is required except in emergency; many Orthodox question baptisms done only by pouring or sprinkling.
Baptism may be by immersion or by pouring (infusion) with the Trinitarian formula; Latin practice usually pours water three times on the head.
Practice varies: Baptists and many evangelicals immerse once and baptize only believers; Lutherans, Anglicans, Reformed and Methodists often pour or sprinkle; some Brethren practice trine immersion.

senses: The twelve major feasts of the Orthodox year celebrating events in the lives of Christ and the Theotokos, ranked just below Pascha.

etymology: Translation of Greek Dōdekaorton "the twelve feasts."

core.definition: The twelve major feasts of the Orthodox year celebrating events in the lives of Christ and the Theotokos, ranked just below Pascha.

pronunciation.tip: Say all three words clearly; "feasts" ends in a quick "sts," which can be hard: practice "feests."

nuance.usage_note: Orthodox Americans speak of "the Twelve Great Feasts" in church school and catechism, and many homes have an icon set of them. They are: the Nativity of the Theotokos, the Elevation of the Cross, the Entry of the Theotokos, the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, the Meeting of the Lord, the Annunciation, Palm Sunday, Ascension, Pentecost, the Transfiguration and the Dormition. Pascha stands above them as the Feast of Feasts.

distinctions.note: Pascha is not one of the twelve; it is the Feast of Feasts above them.
Eight of the twelve are feasts of the Lord; four are feasts of the Theotokos.
A Catholic category of required Mass attendance; it does not match the Orthodox list.

collocations: one of the Twelve Great Feasts
icons of the Twelve Great Feasts
a Great Feast of the Lord

examples.everyday: My daughter is learning the Twelve Great Feasts in Sunday school and can name all of them now.
examples.professional: Each of the Twelve Great Feasts has a forefeast and an afterfeast, ending with the leavetaking.
examples.analytical: The Twelve Great Feasts trace the economy of salvation from the Theotokos's birth to her Dormition, framing the year in Christ's saving work.

nuance.etymology: Translation of Greek Dōdekaorton "the twelve feasts."
common_mistakes: Counting Pascha among the twelve.
Mixing in the Circumcision or Nativity of John the Baptist, which are great feasts but not among the twelve.

senses: Psalms 103 and 146 (102 and 145 in Greek numbering) sung at Liturgy instead of daily antiphons; also a short service replacing Liturgy.

etymology: Greek typika, plural of typikon "according to the type or rule."

core.definition: Psalms 103 and 146 (102 and 145 in Greek numbering) sung at Liturgy instead of daily antiphons; also a short service replacing Liturgy.

pronunciation.tip: Americans usually stress TIP; following the Greek, some say "tee-pee-KAH."

nuance.usage_note: In Russian practice the Typika psalms and the Beatitudes are sung on Sundays as the antiphons of the Divine Liturgy. The Typika service is read when no Liturgy is served, for example by readers in a parish without a priest, and on Lenten weekdays after the Ninth Hour. It is also simply the plural of typikon.

distinctions.note: The typikon is the book of rubrics; Typika are psalms or a service.
Obednitsa is the Slavonic name for the Typika service, "little Liturgy."
Daily antiphons are short refrains with psalm verses; the Typika are full psalms sung in their place.

examples.everyday: Father is away this Sunday, so the reader will lead Typika instead of Liturgy.
examples.professional: On Lenten weekdays the Typika follow the Ninth Hour and precede Vespers.
examples.analytical: The Typika service preserves the shape of the Liturgy of the Word without the Eucharist, a sign of desire for communion.

nuance.etymology: Greek typika, plural of typikon "according to the type or rule."
common_mistakes: Confusing Typika with the typikon book.
Thinking Typika includes Communion; it does not.

senses: A view of the Church as one worldwide body of which local churches are parts, criticized by Nicholas Afanasiev in favor of eucharistic ecclesiology.

etymology: Latin universalis "of the whole" + Greek ekklēsia "assembly" + -logia "study."

core.definition: A view of the Church as one worldwide body of which local churches are parts, criticized by Nicholas Afanasiev in favor of eucharistic ecclesiology.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VER and AH; ecclesiology has six syllables: ih-klee-zee-AH-luh-jee.

nuance.connotation: Neutral as a description; often critical in Afanasiev's use.
nuance.usage_note: An academic term from twentieth-century Orthodox ecclesiology. Afanasiev traced it to St. Cyprian of Carthage and argued that it leads to a universal head of the Church; he opposed to it eucharistic ecclesiology, in which each local Eucharist around its bishop is the whole Church. John Zizioulas later revised Afanasiev's position.

distinctions.note: Eucharistic ecclesiology finds the whole Church in each local Eucharist; universal ecclesiology sees local churches as parts of a whole.
Catholicity is the Church's fullness and wholeness, which Orthodox see in each local church, not only worldwide.
Conciliarity is the communion of local churches through councils.

examples.everyday: Our professor said Afanasiev saw universal ecclesiology as a step toward needing a world-wide pope.
examples.professional: In the essay, Afanasiev contrasts universal ecclesiology with the eucharistic ecclesiology of Ignatius of Antioch.
examples.analytical: Critics argue that Afanasiev's opposition between universal and eucharistic ecclesiology neglects the communion of local churches.

nuance.analogy: Universal ecclesiology sees local churches as branches of a global company; eucharistic ecclesiology sees each as a complete family table.
nuance.etymology: Latin universalis "of the whole" + Greek ekklēsia "assembly" + -logia "study."
common_mistakes: Assuming it simply means "the Church is everywhere."
Pronouncing ecclesiology with stress on CLEE.

senses: The special garments clergy wear during worship, each with its own meaning, such as the sticharion, epitrachelion and phelonion in Orthodoxy.

etymology: Old French vestement, from Latin vestimentum "garment," from vestire "to clothe."

core.definition: The special garments clergy wear during worship, each with its own meaning, such as the sticharion, epitrachelion and phelonion in Orthodoxy.

pronunciation.tip: Stress VEST; the t before m is often barely heard: "VES-munts."

nuance.usage_note: Americans of all churches use it. Orthodox vestments include the sticharion (tunic), orarion (deacon's stole), epitrachelion (priest's stole), zone (belt), epimanikia (cuffs) and phelonion; a bishop wears the sakkos, omophorion and mitre. Western equivalents include the alb, stole, chasuble and dalmatic. Colors change with feasts and seasons.

distinctions.note: "Robes" is a general word; vestments are specifically liturgical clergy garments.
A cassock (rasso) is everyday clerical dress, worn under vestments.
In American English a vest is a sleeveless garment worn over a shirt, unrelated in everyday use.

examples.everyday: The priest wore bright blue vestments today for the feast of the Theotokos.
examples.professional: The deacon recites a verse from the Psalms as he puts on each of his vestments.
examples.analytical: Byzantine vestments developed from late Roman civil dress, gradually acquiring symbolic interpretations.

nuance.etymology: Old French vestement, from Latin vestimentum "garment," from vestire "to clothe."
common_mistakes: Confusing it with "investments."
Using the singular "vestment" for the whole set; Americans usually say "vestments."
nuance.biblical_note: Exodus 28 describes the holy garments made for Aaron and his sons for glory and beauty, which Christian writers saw as a type of liturgical vestments. Revelation 1:13 describes the Son of man clothed in a long robe with a golden girdle.

traditions.view: Clergy always vest for services; each vestment is blessed and put on with a prayer, and the style is shared across Orthodox churches.
Clergy wear vestments such as the alb, stole and chasuble, with seasonal colors set by the liturgical calendar.
Lutherans and Anglicans often wear albs, stoles and sometimes chasubles; Reformed ministers traditionally wear a black Geneva gown; many evangelical and Baptist pastors wear ordinary clothes.

senses: The pattern of Orthodox services that changes by day of the week, each day with its own commemoration, centered on Sunday's Resurrection.

etymology: Old English wicu "week" + Greek kyklos "circle."

core.definition: The pattern of Orthodox services that changes by day of the week, each day with its own commemoration, centered on Sunday's Resurrection.

pronunciation.tip: Stress WEEK and SY; cycle ends in a syllabic l, "kul."

nuance.usage_note: Used in liturgical study and by chanters. Sunday celebrates the Resurrection; Monday the angels; Tuesday John the Baptist; Wednesday and Friday the Cross; Thursday the apostles and St. Nicholas; Saturday all saints and the departed. The hymns come from the Octoechos, which also rotates through eight tones week by week.

distinctions.note: The daily cycle is the order of services within a day (Vespers, Matins, Hours); the weekly cycle is the theme of each day.
The yearly cycle covers fixed and movable feasts over the year.
The Octoechos is the book that supplies the weekly cycle's hymns in eight tones.

collocations: the daily, weekly and yearly cycles

examples.everyday: I didn't know every weekday has its own theme in the weekly cycle until our choir director told me.
examples.professional: Learn the weekly cycle first; it explains why Wednesday and Friday hymns focus on the Cross.
examples.analytical: The weekly cycle makes every Sunday a little Pascha, so that time itself is ordered by the Resurrection.

nuance.etymology: Old English wicu "week" + Greek kyklos "circle."
common_mistakes: Confusing the weekly cycle with the eight-tone cycle, which it contains.
Thinking only Sunday has a commemoration.

senses: The annual round of Orthodox feasts and fasts, combining the fixed cycle by calendar date with the movable cycle tied to Pascha.

etymology: Old English gearlic "yearly" + Greek kyklos "circle."

core.definition: The annual round of Orthodox feasts and fasts, combining the fixed cycle by calendar date with the movable cycle tied to Pascha.

pronunciation.tip: Stress YEER and SY; yearly sounds like "yeer-lee," not "yur-lee."

nuance.usage_note: Used in liturgical study and by chanters. The fixed cycle (Menaion) begins with the church new year on September 1; the movable cycle (Triodion and Pentecostarion) depends on Pascha. Together they shape the weekly and daily services.

distinctions.note: The fixed cycle is the part tied to calendar dates; the yearly cycle includes both fixed and movable.
The movable cycle depends on the date of Pascha.
"Church year" or "liturgical year" is the common everyday phrase for the same idea.

collocations: the Menaion and the yearly cycle

examples.everyday: Living by the yearly cycle, our family always knows what feast or fast is coming.
examples.professional: The yearly cycle begins on September 1, the Indiction, rather than in Advent as in the West.
examples.analytical: The yearly cycle sanctifies time by unfolding the whole economy of salvation within each year.

nuance.etymology: Old English gearlic "yearly" + Greek kyklos "circle."
common_mistakes: Thinking the Orthodox church year begins at Christmas or Advent.
Leaving out the movable cycle.

senses: The traditional unison chant of the Russian Church, written with neume signs called znamena or kryuki ("hooks").

etymology: Russian znamennyy raspev "chant of signs," from znamya "sign."

core.definition: The traditional unison chant of the Russian Church, written with neume signs called znamena or kryuki ("hooks").

pronunciation.tip: Stress ZNAH and pronounce both z and n together at the start.

nuance.connotation: Positive; associated with ancient, prayerful beauty.
nuance.usage_note: Heard in some American Orthodox monasteries and parishes, often in modern staff notation adaptations, and preserved carefully by Old Believers. It developed from Byzantine chant in medieval Rus'. Musicologists and choir directors use the name; most laypeople simply say "Russian chant."

distinctions.note: Byzantine chant uses its own neumes and eight modes with an ison drone; Znamenny is its Russian descendant without the drone.
The Obikhod is the later harmonized Russian chant common in parishes; Znamenny is older and monophonic.
Gregorian chant is the Latin West's plainchant.

examples.everyday: At the monastery they sang the Cherubic Hymn in Znamenny chant, and it was so peaceful.
examples.professional: Our choir is learning a Znamenny chant setting adapted to English by a monastery in Pennsylvania.
examples.analytical: Znamenny chant subordinates melody to text, embodying a theology in which music serves the word.

nuance.etymology: Russian znamennyy raspev "chant of signs," from znamya "sign."
common_mistakes: Thinking it is harmonized choral music.
Pronouncing it "zuh-NAH-men-ee."
